canonical_statement: The systematic review assessed the efficacy, comparative effectiveness, and harms of pharmacological therapies for borderline personality disorder, including subgroup differences.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Our review addressed the following key questions:

canonical_statement: The review searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and PsycINFO through April 6, 2021, and manually searched reference lists.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and PsycINFO

canonical_statement: Eligible populations were patients aged at least 13 years from very-high-human-development-index countries with BPD diagnosed by DSM-IV, DSM-5, or ICD-10 criteria.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Our population of interest were patients 13 years or older

population.label: Eligible BPD study populations
inclusion_criteria: BPD diagnosis based on DSM-IV/DSM-5 or ICD-10
Country with very high human development index

canonical_statement: Eligible interventions were prespecified psychotropic medication classes used for BPD and required at least 8 weeks of treatment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: with a treatment duration of at least 8 weeks

exposures.details: Anticonvulsants, antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, melatonin, opioid agonists/antagonists, sedative-hypnotics

canonical_statement: Prespecified outcomes included BPD severity, BPD-associated symptoms, general psychiatric symptoms, functioning, adverse events, serious adverse events, and withdrawal due to adverse events.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Outcomes of interest included severity of BPD

canonical_statement: Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts; one reviewer extracted data and a second verified accuracy and completeness.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Two reviewers independently reviewed all titles, abstracts, and full-text articles.

canonical_statement: Two independent reviewers assessed risk of bias with Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0, resolving disagreements by consensus or a third reviewer.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: two independent reviewers used the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2.0

canonical_statement: The review graded certainty of evidence with GRADE across risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and reporting bias, with two reviewers resolving differences by consensus.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We graded the certainty of evidence of relevant outcomes based on current GRADE

canonical_statement: When studies were sufficiently similar, the review used restricted-maximum-likelihood random-effects meta-analysis and assessed heterogeneity with chi-square and I-squared statistics.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: we used random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood random effects)

canonical_statement: The evidence corpus comprised 21 randomized controlled trials with 1768 participants; 19 compared pharmacotherapy with placebo and two were head-to-head trials.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Overall, trials included data on 1768 participants.

canonical_statement: Controlled evidence was found for only nine of 87 medications of interest, and no eligible evidence was found for benzodiazepines, melatonin, opioid agonists/antagonists, or sedative-hypnotics.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: assessing nine individual drugs, out of 87 drugs of interest

canonical_statement: Among the 21 included RCTs, two were rated low risk of bias, seven moderate risk, and 12 high risk; high attrition was the main reason for high-risk ratings.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We rated two studies as low risk of bias

canonical_statement: Across included trials, 79% of participants were female, 76% were white when race was reported, and study duration ranged from 8 to 52 weeks.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The majority were females (79%) and white (76% when reported).

population.label: Included trial populations: 79% female; 76% white when reported; duration 8-52 weeks

canonical_statement: Nine double-blind RCTs of second-generation antipsychotics contributed data on 1124 participants.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Overall, these studies provided data on 1124 participants.

canonical_statement: The review rated the certainty of evidence as low that assessed second-generation antipsychotics do not reduce overall BPD severity.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We rated the certainty of evidence as low for no effect

canonical_statement: A random-effects meta-analysis of 497 participants found no statistically significant reduction in depressive symptoms with second-generation antipsychotics versus placebo (SMD 0.28, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.60).
The review rated evidence as moderate that second-generation antipsychotics improve general psychopathology but do not improve functioning.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: moderate for a beneficial effect of assessed second-generation antipsychotics on general psychopathology

canonical_statement: Second-generation antipsychotics were associated with a small higher incidence of adverse events than placebo (67% vs 60%; RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.00-1.21).

population.label: Participants in four RCTs contributing to the adverse-event meta-analysis

canonical_statement: The supplementary random-effects meta-analysis found no statistically significant difference in withdrawal due to adverse events for second-generation antipsychotics versus placebo (RR 1.91, 95% CI 0.83-4.43).

population.label: Participants contributing to antipsychotic withdrawal-due-to-adverse-events meta-analysis

canonical_statement: Nine double-blind RCTs of divalproex sodium, lamotrigine, or topiramate contributed data on 523 participants.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: these studies provided data on 523 participants.

canonical_statement: The review rated evidence as moderate for no effect of lamotrigine and very low for no effect of divalproex sodium on overall BPD severity.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: moderate for no effect of lamotrigine and as very low for no effect of divalproex sodium

canonical_statement: Low- to very-low-certainty evidence suggested that anticonvulsants may improve anger, aggression, and affective lability, but findings were mostly from small single studies with substantial risk of bias.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: studies were small, with mostly high risk of bias, and chance findings are likely.

canonical_statement: The review reports that one divalproex trial found a significant aggression difference on the anger/hostility SCL-90-R subscale (3.0 vs 1.9; p=0.03).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Modified Overt Aggression Scale: 3.0 vs 1.9; p = 0.03

canonical_statement: The review reports that a small lamotrigine RCT found greater improvement in affective lability than placebo (0.71 vs 0.4; p=0.012).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Affective Lability Scale: 0.71 vs 0.4; p = 0.012

canonical_statement: The review reports that a low-risk-of-bias topiramate RCT in 56 women found greater improvement in general psychopathology than placebo (7.4 vs 1.8; p<0.001).
The supplementary random-effects meta-analysis found no statistically significant difference in withdrawal due to adverse events for anticonvulsants versus placebo (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.12-1.89).

population.label: Participants contributing to anticonvulsant withdrawal-due-to-adverse-events meta-analysis

canonical_statement: A small high-risk-of-bias trial of fluoxetine added to dialectical behavior therapy found no significant benefit for anger or aggression; the review rated certainty as very low.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: treatments groups did not reveal any significant differences in anger or aggression

canonical_statement: An unpublished 75-participant fluoxetine trial had suicide-attempt data available on ClinicalTrials.gov, but methodological information was insufficient for formal risk-of-bias assessment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: methodological information provided on ClinicalTrials.gov was insufficient for risk of bias assessment.

canonical_statement: In one 45-participant head-to-head RCT, olanzapine alone or olanzapine plus fluoxetine improved aggression and depressive symptoms more than fluoxetine alone; certainty was rated low.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: significantly greater improvements in aggression

canonical_statement: A 51-participant open-label randomized trial found no significant difference between asenapine and olanzapine for BPD severity, aggression, impulsiveness, or self-harm; certainty was rated very low.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: there were no significant differences in aggression, impulsiveness, and self-harm

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that pharmacotherapies have limited efficacy for BPD overall: benefits, when present, are confined to individual symptoms and are supported by low-certainty evidence.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the efficacy of pharmacotherapies to improve BPD is limited to improvement of individual symptoms

canonical_statement: The evidence base was sparse and fragile: only nine of 87 medications had controlled evidence, most studies were small, many were high risk of bias, follow-up was often 8-12 weeks, and attrition reached 68%.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Up to 68% of participants discontinued the trials.

canonical_statement: Generalizability was limited because trial populations were mostly female and white, no trial enrolled adolescents, subgroup differences were not assessed, and common psychiatric comorbidities were usually excluded.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Not a single trial enrolled adolescents with BPD

canonical_statement: The review found no eligible large long-term observational studies; English-language restriction, publication bias, and selective outcome reporting were additional limitations.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: we could not find any large, long-term observational studies

canonical_statement: The APA Clinical Guidelines Committee assisted in developing key questions, study inclusion criteria, and outcomes, but was not involved in data collection, analysis, or manuscript preparation.
